meta.description: Rilke wrote the poem — but not this sentence. It is a modern condensation; no documented translation reads this way. Earliest instance: a 1993 epigraph.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The purpose of life is to be defeated by greater and greater things'?
meta.ogDescription: Right poet, wrong words: Rilke's 1901 poem carries the idea, but this exact English sentence first shows up in a 1993 book, not in any translation of him.

answer.label: Not Rilke’s wording — a modern condensation
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Rilke’s: it closes a poem he published in German in October 1901, later collected as “Der Schauende” in Das Buch der Bilder. But this tidy English sentence is not his and is not any documented translation of him — the earliest printing of it in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is a 1993 self-help chapter epigraph.
answer.confidenceText: Right poet, wrong words — the poem is real, the sentence is a later paraphrase.

source.excerpt:
Wen dieser Engel überwand,
welcher so oft auf Kampf verzichtet,
der geht gerecht und aufgerichtet
und groß aus jener harten Hand,
die sich, wie formend, an ihn schmiegte.
Die Siege laden ihn nicht ein.
Sein Wachstum ist: der Tiefbesiegte
von immer Größerem zu sein.

Whom this great Angel overcame
That oft the humbler foe rejected,
In light and righteousness erected
From that stern hand goes forth his frame
By molding as of God completed.
No victories can set him free,
His triumph is to be defeated
By ever loftier powers than he.
trail: Rilke published the poem in German in October 1901 in the monthly Deutsche Arbeit under the plain title “Gedicht”, according to Quote Investigator’s citation ↗; the volume’s contents list a Rilke “Gedicht” starting at page 19.

It survives as “Der Schauende” in Das Buch der Bilder, second greatly expanded edition, 1906 — the text is proofread against that edition on Wikisource ↗. The collection itself first appeared in 1902 ↗, with the extended version following in 1906.

Three separate English translators took the closing lines in three different directions between 1920 and 1981, none of them arriving at the popular sentence — all three are set out in the Quote Investigator article ↗.
The exact modern wording surfaces in that same chronology only in 1993, as an epigraph in a motivational book, already stamped with Rilke’s name — see Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The German is the poem’s closing stanza as printed in Das Buch der Bilder (1906), from Wikisource ↗. The English is Ludwig Lewisohn’s 1920 translation, titled “The Seer,” as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from The Nation, 1 December 1920. Neither reads like the quote in circulation.

source.rightsNote: The two texts shown above are safely out of copyright in the United States: Rilke’s German poem was printed in 1901 and collected in 1906, and Ludwig Lewisohn’s English translation appeared in 1920 — all well before 1931. The famous one-line English sentence is a different matter. Nobody has identified who wrote it, and the earliest printing on record is a 1993 book that is still in copyright, so no public-domain status can honestly be claimed for that wording.

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.heading: About Rainer Maria Rilke
author.metaLine: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet & letter-writer, wrote in German
author.bio: Rilke was born in Prague in 1875 and died in Switzerland in 1926, and he is the rare poet whose prose travels as far as his verse — Letters to a Young Poet has probably been pressed into more hands than any book of German poetry. His subject, over and over, is the thing too large to be mastered: the angel, the panther in its cage, the god who will not be bent to human scale. That is exactly why a line about welcoming defeat sounds so much like him even when the words are not his.

misattribution.heading: What is actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this one from Rilke — the idea really is his. What is wrong is the sentence: a smoothed-out English line that no translator of the poem ever wrote, circulating with no source attached.

items.who: “The purpose of life is to be defeated by greater and greater things.”
items.why: It is not a translation of Rilke’s closing lines, which say that a man’s growth is to be deeply defeated by ever greater things — a claim about growth, not a stated “purpose of life.” The earliest appearance in Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ is a 1993 chapter epigraph in James Marshall Galbraith’s Fear of Failure, already credited to Rilke and already in this form.

Ludwig Lewisohn’s “The Seer” ends “His triumph is to be defeated / By ever loftier powers than he”; Jessie Lemont’s “He Who Visions” and Robert Bly’s “The Man Watching” differ again, Bly’s closing on growth “by being defeated, decisively, by constantly greater beings.” All three are transcribed side by side by Quote Investigator ↗, and none produces the popular line.
The Goodreads entry ↗ carries it with over a thousand likes and a bare “― Rainer Maria Rilke” — no poem, no book, no translator. That missing line is the whole problem in miniature.

misattribution.truthLine: Rilke really did write the poem, in German, and it really does end by calling deep defeat by ever greater things a form of growth — you can read the stanza on Wikisource ↗. The famous English sentence is a later compression by an unidentified hand.

context.heading: Why this one keeps getting repeated
lead: Rilke’s poem takes its picture from Genesis: the angel who wrestles with men in the Old Testament. In the German, the fighter who loses to that angel walks away “gerecht und aufgerichtet” — upright and made right — because the hand that beat him was shaping him. The closing line says his growth is being deeply defeated by ever greater things. It is a strange, austere idea, and it does not fit on a mug.

So somewhere along the way it got compressed into one sentence that does. That version reads like a mission statement rather than a poem, which is precisely why it spread through motivational books, commencement speeches and tech-conference slides. Nothing about it betrays Rilke’s meaning — it just is not his sentence, and none of the translators who actually rendered the poem into English ever wrote it.
detailsBody: Tech publisher Tim O’Reilly gave the poem a fresh round of circulation in his 2017 book WTF?: What’s the Future and Why It’s Up to Us, paraphrasing it rather than quoting a translation — and it was that passage, via a tweet from Oliver Burkeman, that prompted Quote Investigator to run the line down in the first place, as the article’s acknowledgements note.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the idea to a Rilke poem printed October 1901 in Deutsche Arbeit under the title 'Gedicht', transcribes the German closing stanza and the Lewisohn (1920, 'The Seer'), Lemont (1943, 'He Who Visions') and Bly (1981) translations, and documents the exact sentence 'The purpose of life is to be defeated by greater and greater things' first in a 1993 chapter epigraph in Fear of Failure by James Marshall Galbraith; it also notes Tim O'Reilly's 2017 WTF? paraphrase and the Oliver Burkeman tweet that prompted the inquiry.
